subject: Immunology
vignette: A 19-year-old college student has had recurrent episodes of sinusitis and two episodes of bronchitis over the past year. He has no other past medical history. Laboratories show undetectable serum IgA (<5 mg/dL), normal IgG and IgM, normal lymphocyte subsets, and normal antibody response to tetanus toxoid. He needs a blood transfusion after a motor vehicle accident.
question: Which of the following is the most important consideration in this patient's transfusion management?

options.text: Routine transfusion is safe because IgA is not present in blood products
He is at risk for anaphylaxis to IgA in donor plasma and should receive washed or IgA-depleted products
He requires irradiated blood products because of absent T cells
He should receive granulocyte transfusions because of neutropenia
He will necessarily develop fatal anaphylaxis with any transfusion

explanation_correct: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and is often asymptomatic, but some patients develop anti-IgA antibodies after exposure to IgA in blood products and can experience severe anaphylactic reactions to plasma-containing transfusions. Washed or IgA-depleted red cells and IgA-deficient plasma minimize this risk. Most patients require no specific therapy, but those with recurrent infections and concurrent IgG subclass deficiency may benefit from immunoglobulin replacement.

explanation_incorrect.A: Plasma-containing products contain IgA, so routine transfusion carries a real anaphylaxis risk in a patient with anti-IgA antibodies.
explanation_incorrect.C: Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in T-cell deficiency; this patient has normal T cells.
explanation_incorrect.D: Granulocyte transfusions are not indicated, since this patient has normal neutrophil counts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Only a minority of IgA-deficient patients have anti-IgA antibodies and react; not all transfusions are fatal or even symptomatic.

educationalObjective: Selective IgA deficiency is usually benign but can cause anaphylaxis to IgA-containing plasma, so washed or IgA-depleted blood products are preferred.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 6-year-old girl with selective IgA deficiency and recurrent respiratory infections undergoes colonoscopy after chronic diarrhea. Biopsy shows nodular lymphoid hyperplasia. A stool sample is positive for Giardia lamblia. She also has a history of mild eczema. Serum IgG and IgM are normal, and IgG subclass testing shows low IgG2.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's susceptibility to Giardia and sinopulmonary infections despite normal IgG levels?

options.text: Selective IgA deficiency abrogates mucosal immunity, and concurrent IgG subclass deficiency impairing responses to polysaccharide antigens compounds it
Absent CD8+ T cells prevent cytotoxic clearance of Giardia
Defective neutrophil chemotaxis reduces granulocyte migration to the intestinal mucosa
Deficiency of terminal complement components prevents MAC formation
Absent thymus causes lymphopenia and vulnerability to opportunistic infection

explanation_correct: IgA is the dominant mucosal immunoglobulin and prevents adherence and invasion of pathogens at respiratory and gastrointestinal surfaces; its loss explains recurrent mucosal infections and giardiasis. Many patients with selective IgA deficiency also have IgG2 subclass deficiency, which further impairs responses to polysaccharide antigens and increases sinopulmonary infection. Treatment is usually supportive, with avoidance of unnecessary immunoglobulin (which itself contains IgA) unless combined deficiency warrants replacement.

explanation_incorrect.B: T cells including CD8+ cells are normal in selective IgA deficiency, so their numbers are not the explanation for this patient's infections.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neutrophil chemotaxis defects describe leukocyte adhesion deficiency, which presents with delayed cord separation and severe bacterial infections.
explanation_incorrect.D: Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9) causes recurrent Neisseria infections rather than mucosal diarrhea and respiratory infections.
explanation_incorrect.E: Thymic absence (DiGeorge) causes severe T-cell lymphopenia and opportunistic infections, not isolated IgA deficiency.

educationalObjective: IgA is the principal mucosal antibody; selective IgA deficiency plus IgG2 subclass deficiency explains mucosal infections including giardiasis.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 31-year-old woman is being evaluated for 8 years of infertility and oligomenorrhea. She has had two episodes of nonmegaloblastic anemia requiring workup and a history of celiac disease. Serum IgA is undetectable, IgG and IgM are normal, and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are absent despite a biopsy confirming celiac disease. Anti-IgA antibodies are detected. She was told as a child that she had a 'mild immune problem' but has had only mild sinus complaints.
question: Which of the following best accounts for the absent anti-tissue transglutaminase result in this patient?

options.text: Celiac disease cannot occur in IgA deficiency, so an alternative diagnosis should be sought
The transglutaminase assay is falsely negative because selective IgA deficiency eliminates the IgA-class serologic marker
Elevated IgG levels in IgA deficiency mask the assay
Terminal complement deficiency consumes the assay reagent
The patient's anti-IgA antibodies cross-react and produce a false positive, not false negative

explanation_correct: Selective IgA deficiency is strongly associated with celiac disease, and celiac serology based on IgA antibodies (anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial) is unreliable because total IgA is absent. In this situation, IgG-based tissue transglutaminase assays or total IgA measurement should accompany celiac screening. IgA deficiency is also linked to autoimmunity and to higher rates of some infections, often remaining asymptomatic, which is why the patient's early history was described as mild.

explanation_incorrect.A: Celiac disease is actually more common in IgA deficiency; the biopsy already confirmed villous atrophy, so the diagnosis stands.
explanation_incorrect.C: Normal to elevated IgG does not interfere with the anti-tTG assay; the problem is the missing IgA class of the autoantibody.
explanation_incorrect.D: Complement deficiency does not affect this immunoassay and has no link to celiac serology.
explanation_incorrect.E: Anti-IgA antibodies in the patient's serum do not create a false positive on a tissue transglutaminase IgA assay; the issue is inability to detect the IgA autoantibody.

educationalObjective: IgA-based celiac serology is falsely negative in selective IgA deficiency, so IgG-based tissue transglutaminase testing is needed to screen those patients.
